analysis.investment_thesis: Aarti Industries has seen a catastrophic earnings collapse — net profit fell from INR 1,186 Cr in FY22 to INR 331 Cr in FY25 — while the stock still trades at 43x P/E, making it both a deteriorating business and an expensive one. With ROE at 6%, EBITDA contracting, and promoter holding below my 55% floor, there is nothing here that meets my quality threshold.
key_strengths: Operating cash flow positive all 5 years — genuine operating business, not purely financial engineering
Long operational history (since 1984) with established customer relationships in specialty chemicals
Revenue CAGR of 10.3% over 9 years shows the business has real scale and some resilience
key_risks: ROE of 6.03% and ROCE of 6.32% are deeply below my 15% minimum — the business is destroying value relative to its cost of capital
Net profit collapsed from INR 1,186 Cr (FY22) to INR 331 Cr (FY25) — a 72% decline — while revenue grew, indicating severe margin erosion and not cyclical timing
Finance costs rising sharply (INR 86 Cr in FY21 → INR 275 Cr in FY25) as debt increases, compounding the earnings problem
red_flags: Promoter holding at 42.14% — well below my 55% threshold; low skin-in-the-game is a disqualifier for me
P/E of 43x on collapsing earnings is egregiously expensive; paying 43x for a 6% ROE business is irrational
CWIP of INR 1,596 Cr (FY25) signals heavy ongoing capex with no evidence of returns — high capex with poor ROCE is a value destroyer
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The numbers for Aarti Industries tell a clear story: this was once a decent specialty chemicals business (INR 1,186 Cr PAT in FY22, ~26% ROE at peak) that has been gutted by margin compression, likely from Chinese competition, overcapacity in the benzene chain, and a sharp rise in finance costs. EBITDA is now trending downward (INR 1,687 Cr in FY22 → INR 986 Cr in FY25) despite revenue growing, which is a textbook sign of a business losing pricing power or structural competitiveness.

I do not invest in businesses where the promoter holds less than 55% — the 42.14% holding here tells me the family does not have full conviction in the long-term outcome. Paying 43x earnings for a business with 6% ROE, contracting EBITDA, and INR 3,973 Cr of debt is not value investing — it is speculation on a recovery that the financials give no basis to assume. I would not own this at any price until ROE returns above 15% and the earnings trajectory reverses convincingly.
